changed.previousSay: Audit a separate constructed cohort. Every request enters together, and we observe everyone through fifteen seconds. One hundred sixty finish by ten. Forty finish later, by fifteen. Fifty are still unfinished. Keep all three groups visible. The unfinished completion times are right-censored: we know they exceed fifteen.

Suppose the report keeps only completed requests. It divides the timely count by two hundred and reports eighty percent. But our question covered every request in the cohort. Bring back the fifty unfinished requests. The denominator is two hundred fifty, and the fraction that finished by ten is sixty-four percent.

The original model put about eighty-two percent before that same deadline. This cohort gives sixty-four. More simulated draws would sharpen the model's answer while leaving this discrepancy. Investigate the shape, request mix, dependence, and waiting process using representative traces. A seed records the experiment; the observations challenge its assumptions.

Your turn. Raise the timer to fifteen seconds. Will ninety-five percent finish? Move the deadline and include the forty later completions. Two hundred of the same two hundred fifty requests finish in time: eighty percent. The remaining fifty still have unknown completion times.

This cohort's completion-time p ninety-five lies beyond fifteen seconds; the log cannot locate it. We began with a median and a timer. Now you can follow a probability area into individual draws, an accumulated estimate, and a measured deadline fraction. Keep the model, the sample, and the unfinished requests in the same story.

beats.say: A random variable describes a quantity whose value will be drawn. Here that quantity is a duration in seconds, so choose positive outcomes. Our supplied lognormal model starts with standard normal noise: a bell-shaped variable centered at zero with standard deviation one.

Multiply that noise by the log-space spread, then exponentiate and multiply by six. Watch a negative noise value become a shorter positive time. Zero becomes six seconds. A positive noise value becomes a longer time. Exponentiation stretches the upper side.

This recipe fixes the median at six and uses a log-space spread of point five five. Its mean is about seven seconds because long waits pull the average upward. These are planning assumptions. We will challenge them against a separate constructed request cohort.

This curve is a probability density. Its horizontal axis is seconds; its height is density per second. Shade the interval from five to seven seconds. The area gives the chance of a reply in that range. The height of the curve alone gives a different quantity.

Bring the two boundaries together at six. The interval gets narrower, and its probability approaches zero, although the density stays positive. A continuous model assigns probability to ranges. A duration rounded to six seconds represents a small interval determined by the clock's precision.

Now sweep from zero to our ten-second deadline. This cumulative area is about eighty-two percent. The remaining area is about eighteen percent: the model's chance that the timer wins. We have an answer under the model. Next, generate individual replies from it.

The cumulative distribution function, or CDF, records the area up to each time. Its height already is a probability. A pseudo-random generator gives us a uniform rank between zero and one. Every equal-width rank interval has equal probability. Use one quarter for our first inspected draw.

Move horizontally from that rank to the curve, then down to the time axis. The inverse CDF turns the quarter-rank into about four seconds. For this lognormal model, we find a standard normal quantile, scale it, then exponentiate. The displayed value comes from that actual calculation.

Try a rank of point nine five. Predict a longer or shorter wait. Follow the same route: it reaches about fifteen seconds. The upper five percent of ranks maps into the whole tail beyond this point. Finite-precision generators and quantile calculations approximate this ideal transformation.

Now use a recorded uniform stream. Each rank becomes a duration and keeps its request identity as it lands in the sample. Blue requests beat the timer; pink requests cross ten seconds. Watch the first five arrive. Each completed arrival adds exactly one to the denominator.

Continue the same stream to twenty requests. The first five stay. Divide the pink count by all twenty to estimate the chance of a late reply. Each late flag is zero or one, a Bernoulli outcome. With independent requests sharing one probability, their total count has a binomial distribution.

Twenty draws are one finite sample from the model, with a rate that can wander. A small sample is especially fragile in the tail. Even when the true p ninety-five is known, twenty independent draws have about a one-in-three chance of containing no value beyond it.

Monte Carlo uses repeated draws to approximate a model's consequences. Here each dot is a separate hundred-request experiment. Its height is the fraction that missed the timer. The dots differ even though every experiment uses the same duration model. The horizontal line is its exact late probability.

Extend every experiment to ten thousand requests. Keep its original hundred and append new draws. Each dot moves to its own newly computed rate. The cloud usually tightens as more outcomes contribute; a particular dot can briefly move farther from the line. More samples steady the estimate without changing the model.

For independent, identically distributed observations with finite variance, the sample mean's standard error scales as one over the square root of the draw count. A hundred times as many draws gives a tenfold smaller scale. Our binary flags have finite variance. Record the seed, draw order, code, and sampler version so this experiment can be replayed.

Keep the median at six seconds, but increase the log-space spread. Keep this inspected random rank fixed too. Watch the high-percentile duration move right as the curve spreads. The middle stays put while the slow experience changes. Predict what happens to the area beyond our ten-second timer.

That late area grows. A repeatable simulation can measure either supplied model very precisely. Choosing the shape requires representative observations. Positive support and a plausible median are useful checks; compare the actual deadline fraction and the slow tail as well. Our next cohort will make that distinction concrete.

Set the spread back to the original point five five. Now put that model aside and open a separate, constructed log. Everyone started together. One hundred sixty finish by ten seconds. Forty finish later, by fifteen. Fifty are still unfinished when recording stops. Their completion times are right-censored. We know they exceed fifteen seconds.

The report divides the timely count by two hundred. Its bracket takes in every request with a recorded finish. Eighty percent looks close to our model. Is that the fraction of arrivals who got a reply by ten seconds?

Bring back the fifty unfinished requests. Each of those people was already waiting at ten. The numerator stays where it was. Now the bracket covers all two hundred fifty arrivals. Only sixty-four percent got a reply in time.

This cohort gives sixty-four percent where the original model gives about eighty-two. Those extra simulation runs can pin down the model's answer as tightly as you like. To explain the gap, check the mixture of requests and the time they spent waiting in representative logs.

The original model puts its ninety-fifth percentile just under fifteen seconds. Someone wants to set the timer there and promise that nineteen out of twenty people get a reply. Use the same log. For ninety-five percent of two hundred fifty arrivals, you'd need at least two hundred thirty-eight finishes. Would a fifteen-second timer have reached that mark?
Move the deadline and include the forty later completions. Two hundred finished by fifteen seconds. The other fifty still have open clocks. We're thirty-eight finishes short of the mark.

The two hundred thirty-eighth finish lies beyond fifteen seconds. The log ends before we can put a time on it. I'd decline the fifteen-second promise on this evidence and follow those open requests to completion. In the next lesson, we'll give two systems the same tasks and ask how much of the difference between them could come from sampling.
